newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-FIS SLAM OFFICIALS OVER PISTE BEHAVIOUR.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-FIS SLAM OFFICIALS OVER PISTE BEHAVIOUR.

text.p: The race director of the Alpine skiing world championships on Wednesday slammed course workers and officials for "scandalous discipline" on the piste during a women's downhill training session.
Kurt Hoch told a team captains' meeting he had seen coaches and technicians slip-sliding down the hill while there were still racers on the piste.
He said even one senior International Ski Federation official was observed skiing down. "If this is the case again tomorrow, I will stop the race," he warned.
Hoch reminded the team captains that an accident at the world championships in Spain last year was caused by a FIS official being on the piste during training.
In that incident, Russian downhiller Tatiana Lebedeva came over a rise at speed and found a FIS official in her path on the piste. Both broke a leg and FIS accepted the blame.
Lebedeva has not returned to ski racing.

In another incident involving officials on Wednesday, Slovenian Rene Mlekuz was made to re-start in the men's giant slalom when his first run was stopped because a course worker remained on the piste shovelling snow.
Mlkeuz had completed about two thirds of the course and did not finish his second run, blaming exhaustion.
A Slovenian team official said that no protest would be made because the damage was done and could not be corrected.
But Norway's Lasse Kjus, the silver medallist, said he would have "hit the guy" if it had happened to him.
"Things like that should not happen. It happened to me once and I wanted to punch the guy," he said. "The organisers should go to the skier and say they are sorry."
Slovenia's Jure Kosir also raised another kind of safety problem before the giant slalom.
FIS secretary general Gian Franco Kasper said officials had inspected his helmet after reports that he had used one with a radio receiver inside it during World Cup races.
"We had some rumours come up that he is using it or had been using it this winter already," he said of the helmet.
"Then we had to check it, we spoke to the coach, we spoke to him and he admitted that sometimes he had used it.

"We cannot go back and punish him for what has happened...but of course we informed him immediately that he is not allowed to do it and we controlled it (the helmet) today at the start with the start referee," Kasper said.
Kasper said the race helmet that Kosir was wearing was without any radio device. Kosir has said previously that he used the radio helmet but without batteries to make it work.

Kasper added that the authorities had an obligation to protect the athlete, arguing that a coach from another team could easily throw him off balance by shouting on the same frequency or making a loud noise.
"On the one hand it's protection and on the other hand it's a prohibition (from using unauthorised equipment)".
